title: Falling Into a Black Hole: What Would You Actually See?
credits: Sources: NASA — Anatomy of a Black Hole; NASA — What Happens When Something Gets Too Close?
disclaimer: Educational visualization based on general relativity. Not a simulation of any specific black hole.
endQuestion: WHAT WOULD YOU WANT TO KNOW ABOUT BLACK HOLES?

scenes.title: The journey begins
scenes.narration: Imagine falling into a black hole. As gravity bends light and time itself behaves differently, the universe around you begins to transform. But what would you actually see as you cross the point of no return?

scenes.title: Finding the black hole
scenes.narration: A black hole is not an empty tunnel in space. It is a region where matter has been compressed so intensely that, beyond a boundary called the event horizon, nothing can escape, not even light.

scenes.title: The accretion disk
scenes.narration: The brilliant light comes from material outside the black hole. Gas and dust heat up as they orbit and gradually spiral inward. The black hole itself remains dark against this spectacular ring of radiation.

labels.sub: Hot gas and dust spiralling inward

scenes.title: Light bends around gravity
scenes.narration: Einstein's theory of general relativity predicts that gravity curves spacetime. Light follows these curved paths, creating distorted images of objects behind the black hole. The sky no longer looks the way it should.

scenes.title: Approaching the event horizon
scenes.narration: As your spacecraft moves closer, escaping becomes increasingly difficult. The event horizon is not a solid surface. It is a boundary in spacetime that separates paths capable of escaping from those that cannot.

labels.sub: A boundary in spacetime, not a surface

scenes.title: Time dilation
scenes.narration: Gravity changes how time is measured by observers in different locations. A distant observer receives light from your spacecraft increasingly delayed and redshifted as you approach the horizon. But your own clock continues to tick normally as you fall.

scenes.title: The photon ring
scenes.narration: Near the black hole, some light can travel along paths that loop around it. These paths create intensely distorted images of the accretion disk and contribute to the thin bright rings around the black hole's shadow.

labels.sub: Light looping around the black hole

scenes.title: Crossing the point of no return
scenes.narration: Now comes the crucial moment. For a sufficiently large black hole, crossing the horizon might not produce a dramatic local flash or visible wall. But once you cross it, no signal you send can escape back to the distant universe.

labels.sub: Locally, the horizon crossing looks unremarkable

scenes.title: Spaghettification
scenes.narration: The difference in gravity between the near and far ends of an object can stretch it dramatically. Scientists call this spaghettification. Around a smaller black hole, these tidal forces can become destructive before the horizon is crossed.

labels.sub: Tidal forces stretch along gravity, squeeze sideways

scenes.title: What lies inside?
scenes.narration: What happens deeper inside remains a profound question. In classical general relativity, a simple non-rotating black hole leads toward a singularity, where the theory ceases to provide a complete physical description. A definitive quantum-gravity explanation remains unknown.

labels.sub: Classical theory stops giving a complete description

scenes.title: What would someone far away see?
scenes.narration: Someone far away would see your signals become delayed, redshifted and dimmer. They would not receive a clear picture of your crossing. Meanwhile, you would pass the horizon in your own finite time, assuming the conditions allow you to survive that long.

labels.sub: Signals arrive later, redder and fainter

scenes.title: Final mystery
scenes.narration: A black hole challenges our understanding of space, time and gravity. We can study its effects, observe its surroundings and test Einstein's predictions. But once something crosses the event horizon, its story can no longer be transmitted back to us. The universe still holds mysteries we have yet to solve.
